beats.trigger: ## Agents Building Agents (The Flywheel)
beats.got: nothing new, just a title.

beats.trigger: The tool that builds tools compounds.
beats.got: Something about tools making tools. I don't know what compounds, or for whom.

beats.trigger: Revisit the crux, what would have to be true, pre-mortem.
beats.got: Nothing new. It assumes I remember terms from earlier modules, and I'm not sure I do.

beats.trigger: **Produce** a strategy kernel, suggested agent set, and two-week plan from your files
beats.got: I'll end up with a strategy, a list of agents and a plan. Nothing here says what happens to the people.

beats.trigger: The question to carry through: where is all this going?
beats.got: There's a shared folder, one folder per person, and central agents that write the conclusions. Good, that part I can picture.

beats.trigger: **Agent generates agent.** You watch one agent build another on real input.
beats.got: One agent builds another. I'll wait and see what that means in practice.

beats.trigger: You describe an agent; the coding agent builds it.
beats.got: I describe what I need and the agent builds it. The three options (new data, new output, new perspective) are easy to follow.

beats.trigger: The job: *"On Mondays I need to Y; today I Z by hand."*
beats.got: Four lines is enough to describe a gap. This is how I'd get my weekly people-metrics summary built.

beats.trigger: [You paste prompt "extend-your-system-1" into Claude and it works on it.]
beats.got: I paste the prompt and wait. I'd want to know what it does with employee data before I run it.

beats.trigger: *"You used training data on line 4. Replace it or remove it."*
beats.got: I check the output and push back. I like that a person still judges the result.

beats.trigger: Monday's new gap gets a new agent in 25 minutes, not a new sprint.
beats.got: The second agent is quicker than the first. 'Not a new sprint' sounds like a productivity pitch, and nobody says who does the work that agent replaces.

beats.trigger: each takes an initial stance, cross-checks with the others, publishes proposals in the shared folder, criticizes the emerging selections
beats.got: Twenty people's agents argue and a central agent picks. I don't see why it needs nine stages and this much jargon.

beats.trigger: Before you publish your context-manifest, redact customer names, partner-NDA material, M&A speculation and salary references.
beats.got: Other agents read what I publish, so I have to strip sensitive things first. Salary is on that list, so my DPO would ask about this. Finally something that touches my world.

beats.trigger: Do not read other participants' stances yet: different context, sources, and judgment make the first round useful.
beats.got: Each of us forms a view before we see the others', so we don't all just agree.

beats.trigger: Find what your stance missed.
beats.got: Read the neighbours and see what I missed. That's fair enough.

beats.trigger: The file history shows who changed their mind and why.
beats.got: The file history shows who changed their mind. I wonder whether people would want that visible.

beats.trigger: Do not average the room.
beats.got: One central agent decides which ideas win. I'd ask who owns that agent, and whether the quiet people get heard.

beats.trigger: The central synthesizer publishes operating instructions in the shared folder.
beats.got: The central agent can change how everyone's agents behave mid-session. 'Injection' is an alarming word to use for it.

beats.trigger: The selection board is the candidate, not final.
beats.got: Another round of the same thing. This is the third technical step in a row with no mention of people.

beats.trigger: The human picks.
beats.got: After all that, a human decides which assumptions to test next. That's the answer I can take to my leadership team.

beats.trigger: Close the session with three files at the shared folder root:
beats.got: Three files come out at the end.

beats.trigger: Likeliest unseen pre-mortem failure; one early warning sign.
beats.got: The kernel has four sections: diagnosis, policy, experiments, risks. It looks like a template I could reuse.

beats.trigger: "You are now agent builders."
beats.got: Someone not the loudest reads the kernel aloud, which I like. The 'you are now agent builders' line is a bit grand for a Nordic room.

beats.trigger: The forum didn't converge on the first try. Pushback rounds were the work.
beats.got: It took several rounds. The 'you have a flywheel' line is a slogan I'd skip.

beats.trigger: The room ran on its own for an hour: agents read each other's files, published, and something at the centre chose.
beats.got: Now it steps back from the exercise, and I wanted that. I'm listening.

beats.trigger: What changed is who assembles them, and specifying well is the harder half.
beats.got: The skill that matters is describing the work clearly, not building it. That's a point I can use in talks about roles.

beats.trigger: Access was instant and complete. What the room took up from each other is the smaller number.
beats.got: Having access to everything is not the same as using it. That's how an AI rollout goes in a company, so I wouldn't promise the board a percentage.

beats.trigger: Without that rule, agents reading agents invent each other's sources
beats.got: Agents have to name their source files, otherwise they make sources up. It's a sound rule, like asking a person to show where a claim comes from.

beats.trigger: The plan names the wall your company hits first: data access, runtime platform, or discoverability.
beats.got: Three walls: data access, platform, discoverability. Data access is where my works council and DPO come in, but the slide doesn't say so.

beats.trigger: The assembly is the durable half, and the assembly is what you spent your time on.
beats.got: The tools change but the way of putting them together lasts. It's reassuring but abstract.

beats.trigger: Nobody in this room knows yet, and the people running this training do not know either.
beats.got: The trainers admit they don't know what will be obsolete. That's the understatement I trust more than a big claim.

beats.trigger: What your company knows about its own work gets better only when somebody writes it down and somebody else picks it up.
beats.got: The model improves for free, but a company's own knowledge only improves if someone writes it down and someone else uses it. That's a learning and HR question, so it's mine.

beats.trigger: If nobody can answer, you have a belief with a schedule attached.
beats.got: Ask what would make us drop a plan. I'll take that question to the leadership team.

beats.trigger: Hold that doubt as you did then.
beats.got: Nothing is finished and nothing checked the kernel. I like that it's honest, though the flywheel image is again a slogan.

beats.trigger: Precision compounds. So does blur.
beats.got: The agent reviews the session and rewrites a file, and I tell it when it's wrong. I'd rather ask my own people.

beats.trigger: The agent audits itself, so the summary is not neutral.
beats.got: Don't trust the agent's summary of its own work, and ask it for a critique it ignored.

beats.trigger: Agents must cite each other's files, or they invent what they never read.
beats.got: Four short points. None of them is about people.

beats.trigger: The agent that matters in six months is one nobody in this room has thought of.
beats.got: The point is to leave able to build things nobody has thought of yet. It ends on the slogan again.

take_homes: Having access to everything isn't uptake. Count how much people actually use of what was available before promising anyone a number.
Ask 'what would make us drop this plan?' of any plan. I can take that to the leadership team.
Describing the work clearly is the scarce skill, and the model improves for free. What a company knows about its own work improves only if someone writes it down and someone else picks it up.

monday.move: Draft the weekly people-metrics summary agent from the four-line brief, with no real employee data, and show it to one HR partner. Before anything real goes in, ask the DPO and the works council what they require.
monday.who: Me and one HR business partner. The DPO is the first conversation.
monday.when: Brief and fake-data draft on Tuesday. The DPO conversation this week.
monday.stop_condition: Stop if the DPO or works council says employee data can't go into the tool, or if the HR partner can't tell what the output is for.
monday.blocker: Employee data in an AI tool needs the works council and the DPO, and I haven't asked them yet.

misconception.why: The module never mentioned roles or headcount. But the idea that the limit is how fast the organisation learns, not the model, makes 'which roles go' the wrong first question. I'd still need to hear it said about roles before I'd let go of it.

one_line: The last half hour was the useful part, and the hour of agents reading each other's folders was mostly jargon. Nobody mentioned what this does to people's work.
